reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Typically presents as an enlarging, firm, hyperkeratotic or crusted nodule or plaque on sun-exposed skin, often tender and prone to ulceration or bleeding
It frequently arises within a field of sun damage, from a pre-existing actinic keratosis, or from Bowen's disease (in-situ SCC)
Unlike basal cell carcinoma, cutaneous SCC carries a genuine, if modest, risk of regional and distant metastasis, so early diagnosis matters
High-risk features include large or thick tumours, poorly differentiated histology, perineural invasion, and sites such as the ear, lip, and non-sun-exposed areas
It arises with particularly high frequency and aggressiveness in immunosuppressed patients, especially organ transplant recipients, and in areas of chronic wounds, scars, or prior radiotherapy
Examine and, where indicated, image the draining lymph nodes as part of staging
Surgical excision with adequate margins is the mainstay, with margin-controlled surgery, radiotherapy, or systemic therapy for high-risk or advanced disease decided in a multidisciplinary setting
Emphasise sun protection, treatment of field damage, and regular surveillance, and consider reducing immunosuppression in transplant patients where feasible
reference.pathophysiology: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is a malignant proliferation of epidermal keratinocytes that have acquired full-thickness atypia and then breached the basement membrane to invade the dermis. Cumulative ultraviolet radiation is the dominant driver, producing signature mutations including in TP53 and other tumour-suppressor and oncogene pathways, with additional contributions from immunosuppression, human papillomavirus in some tumours, chronic inflammation or scarring, and carcinogen exposure. Progression typically follows a continuum from dysplastic keratinocytes (actinic keratosis) through in-situ disease (Bowen's) to invasive carcinoma. Invasive nests of atypical keratinocytes with variable keratinisation can track along nerves and invade lymphatics, giving the potential for metastasis that distinguishes it from basal cell carcinoma.
additionalDifferentials: Keratoacanthoma (rapidly growing crateriform lesion on the SCC spectrum)
Actinic keratosis or Bowen's disease (pre-invasive lesions)
Viral wart or hypertrophic actinic damage
additionalInvestigations: Diagnostic skin biopsy to confirm invasion and assess grade, depth, and perineural involvement
Clinical examination and, when indicated, ultrasound or cross-sectional imaging of regional lymph nodes
Staging imaging for large, high-risk, or node-positive tumours
Multidisciplinary review for high-risk and advanced disease
Assessment of immunosuppression status, particularly in transplant recipients
redFlags: A rapidly enlarging, ulcerating, or bleeding lesion, especially at high-risk sites such as the lip or ear
Palpable regional lymphadenopathy or new neurological symptoms suggesting perineural or nodal spread
A tumour arising in a chronic wound, scar, or previously irradiated skin (potential for aggressive behaviour)
Multiple or aggressive tumours in an immunosuppressed or transplant patient
reference.prognosis: Most low-risk cutaneous SCCs are cured by complete excision, but prognosis worsens with high-risk features such as large size, deep invasion, poor differentiation, perineural involvement, high-risk sites, and immunosuppression, which raise the likelihood of recurrence and metastasis; early detection and adequate treatment are key to good outcomes.
pitfalls: Underestimating the metastatic potential and treating cutaneous SCC as casually as basal cell carcinoma
Failing to biopsy and assess an indurated or growing lesion within a field of actinic damage
Omitting lymph node examination and staging in high-risk tumours
Not recognising the heightened risk and aggressive course in immunosuppressed and transplant patients
management: Complete surgical excision with adequate margins as the mainstay, with Mohs micrographic surgery for high-risk tumours and sites such as the ear, lip and face
Radiotherapy as primary treatment where surgery is unsuitable, or as adjuvant therapy for perineural invasion or incomplete excision
Curettage and cautery or destructive/topical field therapy for low-risk in-situ disease (Bowen's) and actinic keratoses
Nodal assessment with lymph node dissection, and systemic immune checkpoint inhibitors (PD-1 blockade), for advanced, unresectable or metastatic disease
Regular skin and lymph node surveillance for recurrence and new primaries, with staging imaging in high-risk cases
Photoprotection and sun-avoidance advice to reduce ultraviolet-driven new tumours
Review and reduce immunosuppression where possible in transplant recipients, in liaison with the transplant team
Multidisciplinary review for high-risk, node-positive and advanced disease
